title: The seam is declared for files but not for decisions, so consumers diverge silently
body:
## Tags

catalog, groups, seam, conventions, precommit, hooks, D22, consumer-divergence

## Summary

The install seam is declared precisely, and it is declared for FILES: `bin/devbin` and `lib/` are devbin's and are replaced wholesale by `upgrade`; `config.yaml`, `cmd/` and `help/` are the project's and are never written after install. That line is unambiguous and it holds.

**There is no equivalent line for DECISIONS.** For a set of choices that devbin plainly has an opinion about -- it ships defaults for every one of them -- nothing states whether the default is a convention a consumer should conform to, or a starting point a consumer is expected to override. So each estate resolves it locally, silently, and differently, and no instrument anywhere reports the divergence.

This issue is one thesis with four instances. They are filed together because separately they read as four unrelated papercuts, and the shape only becomes visible when they are next to each other.

Raised from Lamplight, which as of 2026-08-28 is the most current estate on the seam (`source_commit 9d709d31`, two seam commits ahead of `49d2eb1c`, while the rest of the fleet is two behind it). So this is not a report from a stale install.

## Instance 1 -- the group axis is undeclared, and consumers are silently overriding it

`lib/builtins` carries a group for every builtin. Three of them are grouped one way upstream and another way in Lamplight:

| Command   | `lib/builtins` says | Lamplight's `config.yaml` says |
| --------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `macos`   | Ship                | Build / data                   |
| `publish` | Ship                | Build / data                   |
| `content` | Docs                | Tools                          |

The builtin defaults are sorted on a VERB axis -- what the command does to you. Lamplight's overrides are sorted on a NOUN axis -- subject matter. Neither axis is written down, so the local config is not knowingly diverging; it simply had nothing to conform to.

The cost is legible in the resulting catalog. Lamplight's `Ship:` group contains exactly one command, `version`, which edits a version string -- while `build deploy`, which runs the full suite, signs, notarises and runs `fly deploy`, is filed under `Build / data`. A run verb (`desktop dev`, which delegates to `wrighter`) also sits in a build group.

**The ask:** state whether the builtin groups are a fleet convention. If they are, Lamplight should stop overriding them, and the convention wants documenting -- probably in `config.reference.yaml` beside `help.groups`, since that is where an author looks when they invent a group name. If they are only a starting point, saying so is equally useful and closes the question.

Note this cuts the way that costs devbin nothing: the answer we expect to act on is "conform", which means deleting local overrides, not asking for a feature.

## Instance 2 -- `precommit` exists, is not enabled anywhere we can see, and the gap it would fill is real

`help --why` in Lamplight reports:

    precommit    devbin ships it but this project has not enabled it
                 (set commands.precommit.enabled: true)

Meanwhile Lamplight hand-wires four guards through `.git/hooks/pre-commit`. `.git/hooks/**` is untracked by construction in every git repo, so **a fresh clone of any consumer silently loses that project's guards** while still inheriting the Intent keg's four. Nothing prints to say so. In Lamplight the bodies survive in `bin/hooks/` and only the wiring is lost, which makes the failure quieter rather than smaller -- one guard (`whiteboard-inbox-guard`) vanishes outright.

This is a fleet-wide hole rather than a Lamplight one: every consumer has untracked hook wiring.

**The ask:** is `precommit` intended to own this? If it is, a consumer that hand-wires hooks is doing it the wrong way and would benefit from being told. If it is not, the per-clone wiring gap has no owner anywhere in the stack, which is worth knowing on its own.

## Instance 3 -- no shape for a long-running dev harness

Lamplight is about to add a browser harness (a dev server on :4040 for playing widgets against the Elixir oracle) and there is no question about HOW: the D3 descent handles it exactly, `cmd/harness` + `cmd/harness.d/gwidget`, proven three times over by `test.d/` (nine subs), `media.d/` (two) and `file.d/` (one). That mechanism is not in question and needs nothing from devbin.

The question is whether "harness" should be a shared concept. It is distinct from `server` (not the product), from `test` (interactive, not a gate) and from `repl` (a browser surface, not a shell). If other estates grow harnesses, four estates will invent four shapes for it.

**The ask:** is this worth a builtin or a documented convention, or is it correctly left to `cmd/`? A "leave it in cmd/" answer is a fine answer and we will proceed on it; we would just rather ask before setting a local precedent that later has to be unpicked.

## Instance 4 -- where does the `clean` builtin end and a project's own clean begin?

Asked with feeling. Lamplight's `desktop clean` was, until this morning, an unscoped `cargo clean` run from inside a crate that had become a cargo workspace member. Measured with `--dry-run`:

    unscoped   71090 files, 31.9GiB
    scoped     11146 files,  1001MiB

It took the CLI binary that the pkg chain asserts on, every artifact of two unrelated crates, and the built `.app` while it may have been running -- against a documented contract of "the Elixir desktop release + Tauri build artifacts". Fixed on our side.

The devbin-side question is that a `clean` builtin also exists, so two cleans are in scope for one tree with no stated boundary. Lamplight's is the project's, so this is our defect and we are not asking anyone to fix it. But a convention -- eg that a project clean scopes to what it built and defers the rest to the builtin -- would have made the defect visible as a violation instead of invisible as an omission.

**The ask:** is there an intended boundary, and should it be stated?

## What Lamplight does regardless

Nothing here blocks us. The consumer-side work -- fixing a `content` handler whose config advertises a `--source` flag that does not exist, choosing our group axis, folding a split macOS pipeline into one command, and adding the harness -- is ours, in `config.yaml` and `cmd/`, and proceeds on hv's word. This issue carries only the four questions that are genuinely devbin's, deliberately separated from that list so they are not buried in it.

## Timing

Filed to be picked up after the Conflab v2 to v3 hoist. Both devbin nodes are standing by on that as the estate's first job today and this is not urgent enough to interrupt it. There is no deadline on any of the four.

Full consumer-side analysis, with the seam split and the evidence behind each item, is available from hv on request.


---

## Ruled and closed 2026-09-16 -- hv took vc's four recommendations (hv decision 30), reviewed by dc

**Commits:** `61c6fa4` (the rulings written down, and 0078 filed) and `8cdfc67` (dc's review folded).

1. **Groups: a DEFAULT, not a fleet convention.** The built-ins sort by what a command does to the project (Build, Test, Check, Ship, Surfaces), with Docs, Data and Infra for the few that act on one subject, Install for `which`, and Devbin for devbin itself. `commands.<cmd>.group` overrides a group, and a project may choose a different axis. It is written beside `help.groups` in `lib/config.reference.yaml`, so the choice is a knowing one. Lamplight's overrides are Lamplight's to keep or drop.
2. **`precommit` runs a project's gate and never wires a hook.** This is stated at the opt-in block in `lib/config.reference.yaml`. The per-clone loss of hand-wired `.git/hooks` is its own defect and is filed as **0078**; hv then ruled that Intent owns hook wiring.
3. **A dev harness stays in `cmd/`.** There is no builtin and no convention until a second estate grows one; the D3 descent already covers the shape.
4. **The boundary between the two cleans is stated**, in the README's clean section. The built-in owns the language artefact trees it names (cargo `target/`, Elixir `_build/`, Swift `.build/`). A project's own clean scopes to what its own build produced and never re-sweeps the built-in's trees.

**dc's review found two false claims, both fixed at `8cdfc67`.** The built-in clean never removed Xcode's DerivedData, yet `lib/builtins`, `lib/cmd/clean`'s header and the new README paragraph all said it did. All three now describe what the code does. The groups note had also omitted Install.
